record.paper_title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
record.original_question: In a network model of a social organization, how can interventions that change selected agents' utilities, signed relations, collaboration costs, or link structure be modeled well enough to reproduce and predict counterintuitive resilience effects such as removal of some agents stabilizing the organization?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a social organization represented as a (possibly signed and weighted) graph G = (V, E, s, w, c), where V is a set of agents, E ⊆ V × V is a set of directed or undirected links, s : E → {+1, −1} assigns a sign to each link (cooperative vs. antagonistic), w : E → ℝ assigns interaction weights, and c : E → ℝ_{≥0} assigns collaboration costs. Each agent i ∈ V is endowed with a utility function u_i : X_i × ∏_{j ≠ i} X_j → ℝ depending on its own action x_i ∈ X_i and the actions of its neighbors in G, and on the structural data (s, w, c). The state of the organization evolves under a specified dynamics (e.g., best-response or noisy stochastic update) that admits one or more equilibria; the "resilience" of the organization is measured by quantitative indicators of equilibrium stability such as the spectral gap of the dynamics, the basin size of the desired equilibrium, the expected time to collapse under perturbations, or the size of the largest cooperating component.

An "intervention" is a transformation T of (V, E, s, w, c, {u_i}) that may simultaneously: (i) modify the utility u_i of a selected subset of agents, (ii) flip signs s(e) of selected links, (iii) change collaboration costs c(e), and (iv) remove or add links or agents (changing V and E). Empirical and case-study evidence indicates that certain interventions exhibit counterintuitive effects—most notably that removing a carefully chosen subset of agents can increase, rather than decrease, the resilience of the organization.

Problem. Construct a tractable mathematical model of the above type (specifying agent state spaces, utility forms, dynamics, and a precise resilience functional R(G, {u_i})) such that:
1. For some explicit network G and choice of utilities, there exists a non-empty subset S ⊂ V with R(G − S, {u_i}_{i ∉ S}) > R(G, {u_i}); i.e., the model exhibits stabilization by agent removal.
2. The model is calibratable to observed organizational data, in the sense that interventions of types (i)–(iv) can be fitted to reproduce given pre- and post-intervention resilience measurements.
3. The model has predictive power: given an unobserved intervention T, the model predicts the resulting resilience R(T(G), {u_i}∘T) with quantifiable error.

Determine such a model, characterize the class of organizational structures and utility configurations under which stabilization-by-removal provably occurs, and identify which subsets S achieve maximal resilience gain.
artifact.status_search_result: Current literature on network resilience, agent-based models of organizations, and counterintuitive removal phenomena (e.g., stabilization via weak-link or selective agent removal, hysteresis in criminal organizations, community-structure effects) describes partial mechanisms and case studies, but no unified, calibratable, and predictive model meeting all three criteria has been established. The problem of building such a model that reliably reproduces and predicts counterintuitive resilience effects from joint interventions on utilities, signs, costs, and topology remains open.

status_evidence.title: Robustness and resilience of complex networks
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of resilience approaches; counterintuitive vulnerability to weak link removal noted but no unified predictive intervention model.
status_evidence.claim: State-of-the-art surveys treat counterintuitive resilience effects as partially understood phenomena rather than fully modeled.

status_evidence.title: Criminal organizations exhibit hysteresis, resilience, and robustness
status_evidence.snippet: Agent-based modeling of criminal organizations shows hysteresis and counterintuitive resilience under interventions.
status_evidence.claim: Specific agent-based models reproduce some counterintuitive effects in particular settings, but generalization is incomplete.

status_evidence.title: Resilience of networks with community structure behaves as if under an external field
status_evidence.snippet: Community structure can remove the resilience phase transition; selective removal can stabilize.
status_evidence.claim: Theoretical results explain how some agent removals can stabilize modular systems, supporting the phenomenon but not providing a fully predictive intervention model.
